Prospero. The protagonist of Shakespeare's The Tempest, a magician-duke who was usurped and exiled to an island. The rightful Duke of Milan, he was deposed by his brother Antonio and cast adrift with his infant daughter Miranda. They washed ashore on an uninhabited island where Prospero spent twelve years studying magic and the occult, developing supernatural power over the island's weather, spirits, and inhabitants. His knowledge grants him near-absolute control over events.

On this island, Prospero binds the spirit Ariel to his service through magic, extracting labor in exchange for the promise of eventual freedom. Their relationship is one of coercion disguised as contractual obligation. He also enslaves Caliban, the island's native inhabitant, subjecting him to servitude and magical punishment. Their relationship encodes colonial power and the justification of colonization through claims of civilizing the savage.

Prospero orchestrates a tempest that shipwrecks his usurper Antonio and other enemies on the island, creating conditions for magical theater and forced reconciliation rather than simple revenge. Yet in the final act, he does something unexpected. Prospero renounces his magic, recognizing that power, even supernatural power, cannot guarantee human hearts or lasting peace. His surrender of magic parallels Shakespeare's own surrender of the playwright's art.

Prospero has been read in many ways. Often he is read as a self-portrait of Shakespeare himself, the artist-magician who controls the stage, manipulates audience emotion, and ultimately acknowledges the illusory nature of theatrical power. Some read him as a colonial master, others as an archetypal figure of authority wrestling with its own renunciation. His arc is the emotional core of The Tempest, and his character represents Shakespeare's alter ego, the artist-creator figure. Through him, the play explores what magic can and cannot do, along with fundamental questions about power, colonization, and the right to rule.
